articles.title: Nvidia posts another blowout quarter as data center revenue keeps surging
articles.subtitle: The chipmaker's revenue more than doubled from a year earlier
articles.excerpt: Nvidia reported fiscal second-quarter revenue of $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year ago, with data center revenue alone reaching $89 billion, and guided to $108 billion for the current quarter as CEO Jensen Huang said AI compute has become 'productive and profitable.'
articles.author: admin

content.text: Nvidia reported another quarter of explosive growth, with fiscal second-quarter revenue coming in at $96.2 billion, more than double what the chipmaker posted a year earlier and roughly 5.7% above the midpoint of its own guidance, as demand for the processors that power artificial intelligence systems continues to outpace supply.
The numbers behind the quarter

Data center revenue, the company's largest and fastest-growing segment, reached $89.0 billion, up 117% from a year earlier and about 92% of total revenue, driven largely by the ramp of Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra chips. Within that segment, revenue from hyperscale cloud providers more than doubled year over year, while revenue from AI-native companies, enterprises and sovereign customers climbed 138%. Gross margin held at 75.0% on both a GAAP and adjusted basis, and the company earned $2.46 per diluted share on a GAAP basis, or $2.22 on an adjusted basis. "AI has reached its inflection point," said founder and chief executive Jensen Huang. "It's doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. Now, compute is revenue. And demand is accelerating."

The company returned $26 billion to shareholders during the quarter through buybacks and dividends, and separately announced a partnership under which Amazon Web Services will purchase two million Nvidia GPUs alongside the company's new Vera CPU. Chief financial officer Colette Kress said capital spending among the industry's five largest hyperscale cloud providers is projected to climb to roughly $1.3 trillion next year, up from about $800 billion in 2026, underscoring how much runway executives believe remains in the AI buildout.
Margin pressure ahead

Kress also flagged that gross margin is expected to decline and bottom out in the fiscal fourth quarter, in a range of 71% to 72%, largely because of rising memory chip costs tied to the broader AI hardware buildout. "We want to be direct about this, rather than let it linger as an open question," Kress said, adding that memory scarcity is being driven in large part by the AI buildout itself rather than by any issue specific to Nvidia.
What comes next

For the current quarter, Nvidia guided to revenue of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, a figure that assumes no data center compute revenue from China, where export restrictions have curtailed the company's ability to sell its most advanced chips; shipments of Nvidia's Hopper-generation products to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue during the quarter just reported. Huang has forecast that revenue will grow roughly 70% in the coming fiscal year, a figure well above what Wall Street analysts had penciled in. Looking further out, the company said it plans to begin shipping its next-generation Vera Rubin platform in the fiscal third quarter, with a larger production ramp expected through the fourth quarter and into early next year, as it pushes further into new markets including autonomous vehicles and robotics.

articles.title: Boeing sells autonomous flight units to Archer Aviation in eVTOL push
articles.subtitle: The deal combines Boeing's drone and airspace technology with Archer's air taxi ambitions
articles.excerpt: Boeing has agreed to sell its Wisk Aero, Insitu and SkyGrid subsidiaries to Archer Aviation in an all-stock deal that will make Boeing one of Archer's largest outside shareholders, with a stake of nearly 20%, as the plane maker continues shedding businesses outside its core commercial and defense operations.
articles.author: ashraf

content.text: Boeing has agreed to sell three of its autonomous flight subsidiaries, Wisk Aero, Insitu and SkyGrid, to electric air taxi maker Archer Aviation in an all-stock transaction, taking a stake in Archer in return and entering a technology-sharing partnership with the company.
Terms of the deal

Under the agreement, Boeing will receive newly issued Archer Class A shares and warrants that will leave it holding roughly 19.75% of Archer's Class A shares, with options to purchase additional shares over the next four years, positioning Boeing as one of the company's largest outside shareholders. Boeing has also agreed to invest up to $55 million in an upcoming Archer funding round and will receive warrants to purchase up to $200 million of additional stock in the future. The plane maker will also be able to nominate a director to Archer's board. The transaction is subject to antitrust review under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act and is expected to close by the end of 2026.
What each side gets

The deal brings together Boeing's work on autonomous drone systems and airspace intelligence software with Archer's push to certify and build electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, a category widely seen as foundational to future urban air taxi services. Wisk has designed, built and flown six generations of autonomous eVTOL aircraft over 16 years and logged more than 1,700 flight tests, while Insitu, which makes high-altitude drones used by militaries worldwide, generates more than $200 million in annual revenue and extends Archer's presence in the defense market. Under a separate cross-licensing arrangement, Boeing will retain rights to use Wisk's core autonomous flight technology in its own commercial and defense aircraft, including in preparations for its eventual successor to the 737.

Archer chief executive Adam Goldstein called the deal "the next big step forward in becoming a diversified platform, rapidly growing our revenue base and bringing scale to our business." Boeing vice president Brian Yutko said the transaction "allows Wisk, SkyGrid and Insitu to accelerate capability development and time to market while ensuring Boeing capitalizes on its investments in these technologies over the past two decades through continued development in our core businesses." For Boeing, the sale continues a divestiture strategy under chief executive Kelly Ortberg, who has directed the company to focus resources on its commercial aircraft, defense and space divisions since taking over in August 2024; Boeing sold its flight-planning and digital aviation unit to private equity firm Thoma Bravo for $10.55 billion last year.
A history between the companies

The agreement marks a notable turnaround in the relationship between Boeing's Wisk unit and Archer, which were locked in litigation as recently as 2021, when Wisk sued Archer over allegations of trade secret theft and patent infringement, including claims that an Archer executive had wiped browsing and download records from a company laptop before joining the startup. That lawsuit was settled in 2023 with Boeing taking a minority stake in Archer at the time. Archer is targeting commercial eVTOL flights by the end of this year or early next, and says the newly acquired autonomous flight technology will support both its urban air taxi ambitions and a hybrid-electric drone it is developing with Anduril Industries.

articles.title: WestJet flight attendants strike, forcing hundreds of flight cancellations
articles.subtitle: The union says unpaid ground work is a central sticking point in negotiations
articles.excerpt: Roughly 4,400 WestJet flight attendants walked off the job on a long weekend after contract talks collapsed, grounding hundreds of flights before the airline and its union reached a tentative deal within a day that includes a 20.5% wage increase over four years and new pay for ground duties.
articles.author: ashraf

toc.text: Part of a broader pattern in aviation labor

content.text: Roughly 4,400 WestJet flight attendants walked off the job in the early hours of August 2, grounding hundreds of flights over a long summer weekend after contract talks between the airline and the Canadian Union of Public Employees broke down.
Why they walked out

CUPE Local 8125, which represents the cabin crew, issued a 72-hour strike notice on July 30 after ten months of negotiations, and WestJet responded with a matching 72-hour lockout notice the same day. The union said members perform roughly 35 hours of unpaid work each month under the airline's existing credit-hour pay system, which does not fully compensate flight attendants for time spent boarding passengers or waiting through ground delays. "We tried until the very last minute to get a fair deal that recognizes the value of the work cabin crews do. WestJet's offer did not go far enough," CUPE Local 8125 president Alia Hussain said in announcing the walkout, which had been backed by a 99.4% strike mandate from union members. WestJet said it canceled roughly 600 flights over the course of the disruption, affecting some 250,000 travelers during the August long weekend.
The deal that ended it

WestJet and CUPE reached a tentative agreement early on August 3, less than two days after the walkout began, though cancellations continued for a time as the airline worked to restore its schedule; more than 300 flights, or about 62% of those scheduled, were still canceled the day the deal was announced. The agreement includes a cumulative wage increase of 20.5% over four years, including a one-time 13% raise retroactive to January 1, 2026, along with a new "duty pay premium" worth roughly another 12% of salary that compensates flight attendants for time spent on ground duties, a $300 annual health spending account and a 13% increase to meal per diem rates in 2026. "This tentative agreement represents meaningful progress," Hussain said. "It evolves the flight credit system by recognizing more of the work cabin crew are required to perform." The deal still requires ratification by WestJet's cabin crew before taking full effect.
Part of a broader pattern in aviation labor

The dispute echoes a similar fight a year earlier at Air Canada, the country's largest airline, where flight attendants struck in August 2025 over nearly identical concerns about unpaid ground work. That dispute ended with a tentative deal that 99.1% of Air Canada's flight attendants went on to reject, before an arbitrator ultimately set the contract's terms in February 2026, largely along the lines of the rejected offer. The back-to-back disputes have added to a wave of contract negotiations across the airline industry this year, as ground staff and cabin crews at carriers in multiple countries press for better pay and working conditions following several years of strong industry profitability.

articles.title: Dick's Sporting Goods shares slide after Foot Locker weighs on earnings
articles.subtitle: The retailer lowered its full-year outlook amid a weakening athletic footwear market
articles.excerpt: Dick's Sporting Goods shares tumbled roughly 30% after the retailer missed second-quarter earnings estimates and slashed its full-year guidance, as its recently acquired Foot Locker business posted a 3.6% decline in comparable sales amid an increasingly promotional athletic footwear market.
articles.author: admin

content.text: Dick's Sporting Goods shares plunged roughly 30% on Tuesday, their worst single-day drop since 2023, after the retailer reported second-quarter results that fell short of Wall Street's expectations and sharply cut its full-year outlook, as its recently acquired Foot Locker business struggles against a weakening athletic footwear market.
A tale of two segments

The company's core Dick's-branded stores delivered comparable sales growth of 4.9% for the quarter, with average ticket size up 3.6% and transactions up 1.3%, driven by broad-based gains across categories and a tailwind from this year's FIFA World Cup. Foot Locker told a very different story: proforma comparable sales at the chain declined 3.6%, which executive chairman Ed Stack attributed to "conditions across portions of the athletic footwear and apparel marketplace" that grew increasingly promotional as the quarter progressed, along with fewer new sneaker launches that also underperformed both industry and company expectations. Stack said the environment hit Foot Locker harder than the core Dick's business given its heavier reliance on legacy footwear styles and retro product releases.
The numbers

Consolidated net sales rose 53.2% to $5.59 billion, short of the $5.65 billion analysts had expected, with the increase driven almost entirely by the roughly $1.74 billion contribution from Foot Locker, which Dick's acquired for $2.4 billion in a deal that closed in September 2025. Net income for the quarter was $315 million, or $3.50 per diluted share, down from $381 million, or $4.71 per share, a year earlier; adjusted earnings per share of $3.53 missed the $3.78 consensus estimate. Gross margin fell to 34.8% from 37.1% a year ago, a decline the company attributed to Foot Locker, even as the core Dick's segment's own margin expanded. Chief executive Lauren Hobart said the company remains "highly confident in the strength of the Dick's Business and our long-term opportunity at Foot Locker," even while taking "a more cautious view of the balance of the year."
A steep guidance cut

Dick's lowered its full-year adjusted earnings guidance to a range of $11.00 to $12.00 per share, down from a prior range of $13.27 to $14.27 and well below the $14.20 analysts had been expecting, a roughly 19% shortfall at the midpoint. The company narrowed its full-year sales outlook to a range of $21.9 billion to $22.2 billion and now expects Foot Locker's proforma comparable sales for the year to fall somewhere between a 2% decline and flat growth, compared with previous expectations for growth, while maintaining its outlook for the core Dick's business at 2.5% to 4% comparable sales growth. The company also disclosed it received $59 million in tariff refunds during the quarter, along with $2.1 million in related interest income, though that was not enough to offset the broader concerns driving the stock's decline.

articles.title: Alibaba to sell videogame business in strategic portfolio shift
articles.subtitle: The sale is valued at more than $1.5 billion
articles.excerpt: Alibaba has agreed to sell its gaming studio, Lingxi Games, to Asian private equity firm Trustar Capital in a deal valued at more than $1.5 billion, deepening a pivot toward artificial intelligence infrastructure that chief executive Eddie Wu has said will exceed the company's original $53 billion AI spending plan.
articles.author: admin

content.text: Alibaba has agreed to sell its gaming studio, Lingxi Games, to Asian private equity firm Trustar Capital in a deal Bloomberg valued at no less than $1.5 billion, the latest step in a broader effort by the Chinese technology conglomerate to shed non-core businesses and redirect resources toward artificial intelligence.
The deal

Under the agreement, disclosed in an internal memo that Lingxi chief executive Zhou Bingshu sent to staff, Alibaba will transfer its entire stake in the studio to Trustar Capital, formerly known as CITIC Capital, taking the Chinese tech giant fully out of in-house game development. Reuters reported, citing a person familiar with the matter, that Alibaba stands to collect more than $2 billion from the sale. Guangzhou-based Lingxi is best known for "Three Kingdoms: Strategy Edition," a multiplayer strategy title it developed with Japan's Koei Tecmo Holdings. Several publicly listed Chinese gaming companies, including 37 Interactive Entertainment, China Ruyi, Century Huatong and Giant Network, had entered the bidding process after Alibaba formally put the studio up for sale in June, with Trustar ultimately prevailing by outbidding the strategic industry buyers. Zhou and Lingxi's existing leadership are expected to remain in place under the new ownership.
Why now

The sale is part of what Alibaba has described as a "slimming down" strategy under chief executive Eddie Wu, who has already overseen the divestment of Intime Department Store and Sun Art Retail this year as the company concentrates resources on e-commerce, cloud computing and artificial intelligence. Alibaba said in February 2025 that it planned to invest more than 380 billion yuan, or roughly $56.4 billion, in cloud and AI infrastructure over three years; Wu has since said that spending will exceed the original figure. The move mirrors a broader retreat from gaming across China's biggest internet platforms: ByteDance sold its Moonton Technology gaming unit to Savvy Games Group, a subsidiary of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, for more than $6 billion in March, and Tencent has been scaling back its own overseas gaming studio footprint. Analysts say the shift reflects both the heavy capital demands of AI infrastructure and the fact that traditional gaming companies increasingly lack the financial firepower to compete with private equity buyers for studios like Lingxi.
